statements.quote: A single text prompt, and a diffusion model produced this image in seconds.
This one was created with the prompt “Astronaut Riding a Horse” (\cite[Image: Stable Diffusion 3.5]{diffusion_astronaut_img})
Ask a model for “a photograph of an astronaut riding a horse” and it hands back a convincing image that never existed.
That is the job of a **generative model**: learn the statistical structure of images well enough to sample new ones.
For years the job was done by several competing recipes.
**Generative adversarial networks** (GANs) trained a generator and a discriminator against each other; they produced sharp images but were notoriously unstable to train.
**Variational autoencoders** (VAEs) squeezed an image into a small latent code and decoded it back; they were stable but often blurry.
**Autoregressive models** predicted pixels or discrete image tokens one at a time, which was flexible but slow.
Getting any of these to work well took care and patience.

Then in 2020, a paper called **DDPM** (\cite[Ho et al., 2020]{ho2020ddpm}) turned a 2015 idea from Jascha Sohl-Dickstein and colleagues (\cite[Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015]{sohl2015deep}) into a practical recipe: learn to reverse a fixed noising process.

A parallel line, score-based generation (\cite[Song & Ermon, 2019]{song2019score}), was learning to push random samples toward more likely images, and it converged on the same destination from the other side.
Within two years, Stable Diffusion, DALL·E 2, Imagen, and Midjourney had made **diffusion** the dominant way to generate images.
By 2024 it had spread to video (Sora, Veo), audio, music, and even 3D protein structures.
The idea is almost paradoxical.
Instead of generating an image in one forward pass, a diffusion model **destroys an image with noise step by step, then learns to undo the destruction, one tiny step at a time**.
It is a different paradigm from the word-by-word prediction used by chatbots, even though both produce striking results.
The idea is older than the image generators that made it famous.

\cite[Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015)]{sohl2015deep} introduced diffusion probabilistic models in 2015 as a way to learn a generative distribution by reversing a process that gradually destroys structure.
The method worked on small datasets but was expensive and did not beat the generative models of the day.
Its revival waited for a better training objective and a better architecture.
Not every system in that wave was a diffusion model.
**DALL·E** (2021) was a 12-billion-parameter autoregressive Transformer over discrete image tokens, a direct application of the language-model recipe to pixels.

**DALL·E 2** then switched to diffusion conditioned on CLIP *text* embeddings, where CLIP is a separate network that learns a shared vector space for text and images, and the rest of the field followed (\cite[Ramesh et al., 2022]{ramesh2022dalle2}); the 2021 DALL·E paper describes the earlier autoregressive system (\cite[Ramesh et al., 2021]{ramesh2021dalle}).
DALL·E's detour is a useful reminder that “predict the next token” is architecture-agnostic: the token can be a word, an image patch, or an audio frame.

statements.quote: If you would rather read the foundational papers, the trio that started it all is Sohl-Dickstein's 2015 thermodynamic framing (\cite[Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015]{sohl2015deep}), Song & Ermon's score-based 2019 paper (\cite[Song & Ermon, 2019]{song2019score}), and Ho's DDPM in 2020 (\cite[Ho et al., 2020]{ho2020ddpm}).
statements.section: Try it yourself

blocks.quote: A single text prompt, and a diffusion model produced this image in seconds. This one was created with the prompt “Astronaut Riding a Horse” (\cite[Image: Stable Diffusion 3.5]{diffusion_astronaut_img})

Ask a model for “a photograph of an astronaut riding a horse” and it hands back a convincing image that never existed. That is the job of a **generative model**: learn the statistical structure of images well enough to sample new ones.

For years the job was done by several competing recipes. **Generative adversarial networks** (GANs) trained a generator and a discriminator against each other; they produced sharp images but were notoriously unstable to train. **Variational autoencoders** (VAEs) squeezed an image into a small latent code and decoded it back; they were stable but often blurry. **Autoregressive models** predicted pixels or discrete image tokens one at a time, which was flexible but slow. Getting any of these to work well took care and patience.

Then in 2020, a paper called **DDPM** (\cite[Ho et al., 2020]{ho2020ddpm}) turned a 2015 idea from Jascha Sohl-Dickstein and colleagues (\cite[Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015]{sohl2015deep}) into a practical recipe: learn to reverse a fixed noising process. A parallel line, score-based generation (\cite[Song & Ermon, 2019]{song2019score}), was learning to push random samples toward more likely images, and it converged on the same destination from the other side. Within two years, Stable Diffusion, DALL·E 2, Imagen, and Midjourney had made **diffusion** the dominant way to generate images. By 2024 it had spread to video (Sora, Veo), audio, music, and even 3D protein structures.

The idea is almost paradoxical. Instead of generating an image in one forward pass, a diffusion model **destroys an image with noise step by step, then learns to undo the destruction, one tiny step at a time**. It is a different paradigm from the word-by-word prediction used by chatbots, even though both produce striking results.

The idea is older than the image generators that made it famous. \cite[Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015)]{sohl2015deep} introduced diffusion probabilistic models in 2015 as a way to learn a generative distribution by reversing a process that gradually destroys structure. The method worked on small datasets but was expensive and did not beat the generative models of the day. Its revival waited for a better training objective and a better architecture.

Not every system in that wave was a diffusion model. **DALL·E** (2021) was a 12-billion-parameter autoregressive Transformer over discrete image tokens, a direct application of the language-model recipe to pixels. **DALL·E 2** then switched to diffusion conditioned on CLIP *text* embeddings, where CLIP is a separate network that learns a shared vector space for text and images, and the rest of the field followed (\cite[Ramesh et al., 2022]{ramesh2022dalle2}); the 2021 DALL·E paper describes the earlier autoregressive system (\cite[Ramesh et al., 2021]{ramesh2021dalle}). DALL·E's detour is a useful reminder that “predict the next token” is architecture-agnostic: the token can be a word, an image patch, or an audio frame.
The diffusion process
blocks.section: The diffusion process

blocks.quote: The central trick: destroy, then learn to undo
blocks.section: The central trick: destroy, then learn to undo

blocks.quote: Imagine dropping a clear photograph into a glass of water and slowly stirring in drops of black ink. After each drop the picture becomes a little less recognizable. After enough drops, all you see is uniform grey.
blocks.section: The central trick: destroy, then learn to undo

blocks.quote: Now imagine the reverse: starting with grey water, learn to *remove* exactly the right amount of ink, drop by drop, until a coherent photograph reappears. If you can learn that reverse process well enough, you can start from *any* grey water and turn it into a fresh, novel photograph.
blocks.section: The central trick: destroy, then learn to undo

blocks.quote: That is what a diffusion model does. The forward process (ink going in) is a hand-designed procedure with no learned parameters. The reverse process (ink coming out) is what a neural network has to learn.
blocks.section: The central trick: destroy, then learn to undo

blocks.quote: The forward process: a controlled demolition
blocks.section: The forward process: a controlled demolition

blocks.quote: The slider below shows the forward process happening to a real image. Drag it to watch the picture dissolve into noise.
blocks.section: The forward process: a controlled demolition

blocks.quote: The reverse process: the part that learns
blocks.section: The reverse process: the part that learns

blocks.quote: The reverse process starts from pure noise and runs backward. At each step, the network looks at the current noisy image and asks: *what noise should I subtract to make this slightly more recognizable?* A thousand such tiny denoising steps, and out pops a clean image.
blocks.section: The reverse process: the part that learns

blocks.quote: DDPM's contribution was to make the reverse chain trainable with a simple surrogate. Instead of predicting the full reverse distribution, the network predicts the noise that was added, and training minimizes squared error to it. That objective is a reweighted variational bound, and the reweighting is what made sample quality jump (\cite[Ho et al., 2020]{ho2020ddpm}). \cite[Nichol & Dhariwal (2021)]{nichol2021improved} then replaced the linear noise schedule with a cosine one and learned the reverse variances, improving both log-likelihood and sample quality. \cite[Dhariwal & Nichol (2021)]{dhariwal2021diffusion} added classifier guidance and showed diffusion could beat GANs on image synthesis.
blocks.section: The reverse process: the part that learns

blocks.quote: 3. Ask the network to predict *what that noise was*.
blocks.section: The reverse process: the part that learns

blocks.quote: 4. Train by mean-squared error between the predicted and the true noise.
blocks.section: The reverse process: the part that learns

blocks.quote: For the vanilla DDPM objective, that is it: no discriminator, no generator, no min-max game. DDIM is a *sampler* for a DDPM-trained model, not a separate training recipe, so the same objective applies (\cite[Song et al., 2020]{song2020ddim}). In both cases the loss is just MSE between predicted and true noise. This stability is one of the big reasons diffusion displaced GANs so quickly. (One caveat: the 1-step “Turbo” models like SDXL-Turbo were *not* trained with pure MSE. They use **adversarial diffusion distillation**, an explicit GAN-style loss, to compress 50 denoising steps into 1.)
blocks.section: The reverse process: the part that learns

blocks.quote: The slider below steps through the **reverse** process on the same image. Drag it from right to left to watch an image emerge from chaos. In a real diffusion model this would take a thousand tiny denoising steps; here we collapse them into a handful of frames.
blocks.section: The reverse process: the part that learns

blocks.quote: Why does this work?
blocks.section: Why does this work?

blocks.quote: You might ask: how can *removing noise* ever create a picture? The answer is that **a denoiser that can spot noise must also have learned what “no noise” looks like**. It has implicitly learned the shape of the data distribution. If you start from pure noise and repeatedly denoise, each step moves you toward a more likely image, and you end up with a brand new sample.
blocks.section: Why does this work?

blocks.quote: Two ways to make this concrete:
blocks.section: Why does this work?

blocks.quote: Both views say the same thing: a good denoiser is also a generative model.
blocks.section: Why does this work?

blocks.quote: The denoising and score-matching lineages were unified in 2021. \cite[Song et al. (2021)]{song2021sde} showed that both are discretizations of a stochastic differential equation, a differential equation with randomness: a forward SDE adds noise, and a reverse-time SDE, driven by the score, removes it. That view made the sampler a design choice rather than a consequence of the training chain. \cite[Song et al. (2020)]{song2020ddim} had already shown the point concretely: a deterministic reverse process that can skip steps samples a DDPM model in far fewer steps with little loss in quality.
blocks.section: Why does this work?

blocks.quote: Conditioning and the model
blocks.section: Conditioning and the model

blocks.quote: Telling the model what to draw
blocks.section: Telling the model what to draw

blocks.quote: A diffusion model needs a signal that tells it what to draw. For text-to-image, that signal is a text prompt, first encoded into a sequence of token vectors by a separate text encoder (typically CLIP or T5).
blocks.section: Telling the model what to draw

blocks.quote: Guidance began with a classifier. \cite[Dhariwal & Nichol (2021)]{dhariwal2021diffusion} showed that the gradient of a pretrained image classifier could steer each denoising step toward a chosen class. That trick, classifier guidance, improved sample quality at the cost of an extra network. \cite[Ho & Salimans (2022)]{ho2022cfg} removed the classifier: train one denoiser with the condition randomly dropped, then extrapolate away from its unconditional prediction. Stable Diffusion uses this version because it needs no classifier and works with free-form text.
blocks.section: Telling the model what to draw

blocks.quote: The version most text-to-image models use is **classifier-free guidance**. At training time, the network is shown the text prompt 90% of the time and *nothing* 10% of the time, so it learns both a conditional and an unconditional denoiser in one model. At inference, you amplify the gap between them:
blocks.section: Telling the model what to draw

blocks.quote: From text to image: the whole pipeline
blocks.section: From text to image: the whole pipeline

blocks.quote: Classifier-free guidance explains how to amplify the prompt. Three questions remain: **where do the (image, prompt) training pairs come from?**, **how does the text encoder turn words into something the U-Net can read?**, and **how does the U-Net use those numbers?** The rest of this section walks through the pipeline end-to-end.
blocks.section: From text to image: the whole pipeline

blocks.quote: 1. Training data, no manual labels needed
blocks.section: 1. Training data, no manual labels needed

blocks.quote: You do **not** need to label 100,000 images by hand. The training set for Stable Diffusion is **LAION-5B**, a publicly released scrape of about 5 billion (image, alt-text) pairs from the web. The “label” of every image is whatever its surrounding HTML already said: the alt attribute, the caption, the page title.
blocks.section: 1. Training data, no manual labels needed

blocks.quote: What the model learns from this data is **not a database of specific images**. It learns an *internal representation of the world*: what astronauts look like, what horses look like, what “riding” looks like, what “in space” looks like, each concept distilled from many thousands of images seen during training. When you prompt for “an astronaut riding a horse”, there is almost certainly no training image of exactly that scene. The model composes a new image by combining its learned concepts: astronaut-shape here, horse-shape there, riding-pose between them. The output is **synthesized**, not retrieved.
blocks.section: 1. Training data, no manual labels needed

blocks.quote: This is also why diffusion models sometimes hallucinate or get details wrong: the “labels” are noisy, scraped web text, not clean annotations, and the concepts are statistical, not encyclopedic.
blocks.section: 1. Training data, no manual labels needed

blocks.quote: (One consequence: as more AI-generated images flood the web, future models trained on the same web will be trained on their own predecessors' outputs. This recursive phenomenon is called **model collapse**, and it is a real research concern.)
blocks.section: 1. Training data, no manual labels needed

blocks.quote: 2. Text becomes numbers, the text encoder and embeddings
blocks.section: 2. Text becomes numbers, the text encoder and embeddings

blocks.quote: The diffusion U-Net cannot read English. Before it ever sees your prompt, a separate **text encoder** turns the prompt into a sequence of vectors. For Stable Diffusion 1.5, that encoder is CLIP's text tower; SD 3 combines CLIP-L, CLIP-G and T5-XXL, and FLUX combines CLIP-L with T5-XXL. All of these encoders are **Transformers**, the same architecture family as the LLMs in the other chapters.
blocks.section: 2. Text becomes numbers, the text encoder and embeddings

blocks.quote: The text encoder does two things, in order: tokenization and embedding. Both are covered in detail elsewhere on this site (see the **Tokenization** and **Embeddings** chapters); the small viz above is just a quick reminder of what comes out of the other end of that pipeline. The crucial property for our purposes is that each token ends up as a vector (768 numbers for CLIP, 4096 for T5-XXL), and **similar concepts end up close together** in that vector space: “astronaut” and “space suit” have nearby vectors, “horse” and “pony” have nearby vectors, “astronaut riding a horse” is far from “still life with fruit”.
blocks.section: 2. Text becomes numbers, the text encoder and embeddings

blocks.quote: 3. Cross-attention, how the U-Net reads the text
blocks.section: 3. Cross-attention, how the U-Net reads the text

blocks.quote: Now the diffusion U-Net has two inputs at every denoising step:
blocks.section: 3. Cross-attention, how the U-Net reads the text

blocks.quote: The U-Net applies **cross-attention** in its attention blocks. The intuition: **at every step, the model paints the image by asking each word in your prompt, “which part of the picture is yours?”** The word *“astronaut”* claims the upper-center region. The word *“horse”* claims the lower region. The word *“riding”* claims the bit in between. Function words like *“a”*, *“of”* barely claim anything.
blocks.section: 3. Cross-attention, how the U-Net reads the text

blocks.quote: In the demo below, click any *content* word in the prompt and watch a colored region light up over the part of the astronaut image that word would “claim” during generation. The regions are simplified; a real diffusion model has hundreds of tiny patches, but the principle is the same: each word in your prompt controls its own piece of the picture.
blocks.section: 3. Cross-attention, how the U-Net reads the text

blocks.quote: Cross-attention is how Stable Diffusion connects words to image regions. Different words control different regions. By the end of denoising, each pixel of the image has been “asked” which word it should look like, and the text embedding has answered. **If you swap one word in the prompt, the embedding moves, the attention shifts, and the region that word controls changes most.** The full Stable Diffusion pipeline looks like this end-to-end:
blocks.section: 3. Cross-attention, how the U-Net reads the text

blocks.quote: The Stable Diffusion pipeline: a text encoder turns your prompt into vectors, the U-Net denoises a latent tensor conditioned on those vectors (via cross-attention), and a frozen VAE decoder turns the clean latent back into pixels. \cite[Image: Stable Diffusion architecture]{diffusion_architecture_img}
blocks.section: 3. Cross-attention, how the U-Net reads the text

blocks.quote: So the answer to “do I need to label 100k images?” is: **no** for pretraining, because the labels already exist on the web. The yes cases are *fine-tuning*: if you want the model to draw a specific style or subject, you can fine-tune with **LoRA** (\cite[Hu et al., 2021]{hu2021lora}) on as few as a few dozen images, or steer outputs with **ControlNet** (\cite[Zhang et al., 2023]{zhang2023controlnet}) using edge maps, depth maps, or pose skeletons.
blocks.section: 3. Cross-attention, how the U-Net reads the text

blocks.quote: What's the network?
blocks.section: What's the network?

blocks.quote: The denoiser's architecture is borrowed from medical imaging. The **U-Net** was introduced by \cite[Ronneberger et al. (2015)]{ronneberger2015unet} for biomedical segmentation. Its contracting path captures context; its symmetric expanding path restores fine detail; skip connections pass high-resolution features across. The resulting architecture is shaped like a U: it first downsamples the image, then upsamples it back. Diffusion models adopted it because denoising is also a dense, image-to-image prediction: every latent cell needs an output, and coarse structure and fine texture must be combined. \cite[Nichol & Dhariwal (2021)]{nichol2021improved} and \cite[Dhariwal & Nichol (2021)]{dhariwal2021diffusion} then tuned this backbone with residual blocks, attention and time embeddings.
blocks.section: What's the network?

blocks.quote: Stable Diffusion: doing it in a compressed space
blocks.section: Stable Diffusion: doing it in a compressed space

blocks.quote: Doing all this in raw pixel space at $512 \times 512$ resolution is expensive. Each image is roughly 786,000 numbers, and every one of them has to pass through dozens of layers at every denoising step.
blocks.section: Stable Diffusion: doing it in a compressed space

blocks.quote: Compression had a long history in generative modeling. Autoencoders had long learned compact codes (\cite[Kingma & Welling, 2014]{kingma2014vae}), and VQGAN showed that a discrete autoencoder plus a powerful prior could synthesize high-resolution images (\cite[Esser et al., 2021]{esser2021taming}). \cite[Rombach et al. (2022)]{rombach2022ldm} made the decisive move for diffusion: train the autoencoder first, freeze it, and run the diffusion process entirely in its latent space. That made training cheaper. It also let the same denoiser scale to larger images by changing only the decoder.
blocks.section: Stable Diffusion: doing it in a compressed space

blocks.quote: The key idea of **Latent Diffusion Models** (\cite[Rombach et al., 2022]{rombach2022ldm}), the technology behind Stable Diffusion, is to *first* compress the image into a much smaller latent representation using a pretrained autoencoder, *then* do all the diffusion work in that compressed space, *then* decode the result back to pixels. The U-Net never sees a pixel; it only sees a $64 \times 64$ latent map. This makes training and inference roughly 64× cheaper.
blocks.section: Stable Diffusion: doing it in a compressed space

blocks.quote: In Stable Diffusion 1.5, the text prompt goes through CLIP, the latent goes through the U-Net, and at the end a frozen VAE decoder turns the clean latent back into an image. The VAE is never trained alongside the diffusion model; it was learned earlier as an ordinary autoencoder and frozen in place.
blocks.section: Stable Diffusion: doing it in a compressed space

blocks.quote: The figure below shows a real Stable Diffusion 1.5 run using DDIM sampling. Read it from top-left to bottom-right: the network starts from pure noise and gradually reveals a coherent image of a European-style castle in Japan, adding detail with each step.
blocks.section: Stable Diffusion: doing it in a compressed space

blocks.quote: Each frame is one denoising step of a Stable Diffusion 1.5 model using DDIM sampling. Early steps establish rough shapes and color fields; later steps refine texture and fine detail. \cite[Image: DDIM denoising steps]{diffusion_ddim_img}

blocks.section: Beyond images

blocks.quote: The same recipe works anywhere you can define a “noising” process and a network that can reverse it:
blocks.section: Beyond images

blocks.quote: The general principle is simple: **if you can blur it, you can unblur it; and if you can unblur it, you can generate it from scratch.**
blocks.section: Beyond images

blocks.quote: Where the field is now
blocks.section: Where the field is now

blocks.quote: By 2025, many new systems use **flow matching** (\cite[Lipman et al., 2023]{lipman2023flow}) or its rectified-flow variant, in which the path between data and noise is trained to be straighter than the curved diffusion path. FLUX and Stable Diffusion 3 use rectified flow; DDPM/DDIM-style samplers remain widespread in older and distilled models.
blocks.section: Where the field is now

blocks.quote: The dominant backbone is no longer the U-Net but the **Diffusion Transformer (DiT)** (\cite[Peebles & Xie, 2023]{peebles2023dit}), a vanilla Vision Transformer scaled up. Sora, FLUX, and Stable Diffusion 3 all use DiT-style backbones. The pattern is familiar: U-Net worked, then Transformers worked better once they were big enough.
blocks.section: Where the field is now

blocks.quote: Practical models have also become fast. Modern systems generate images in **1 to 8 network evaluations** through clever solvers (DPM-Solver, EDM) and adversarial distillation (SDXL-Turbo, LCM). Diffusion is no longer slow.
blocks.section: Where the field is now
